data.title: Vance casts doubt on Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution
data.description:
Vance expresses doubts about Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution

Associated Press
Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 5:33 PM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it."

The Republican vice president said, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan's crimes should not be forgotten.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the Republican said.

Advertisement

"Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it," he said.

Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting "the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it."

Trump called Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009, "a maniac."

Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn't mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it.

___

This story has been corrected to show the military base's name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood.

data.title: New Paxton recording exposes lingering GOP divisions in a tight Texas Senate race
data.description:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks during a campaign event in Houston, on September 21.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Ken Paxton has publicly said he would “love to have” John Cornyn’s support after their bruising Republican primary runoff in the Texas Senate race. But privately, Paxton has grown frustrated with the outgoing senator’s distance from his campaign.

“He’s clearly not helping. He wants me to lose,” the Texas attorney general said at a fundraiser last month, according to an audio recording obtained by CNN from an attendee who opposes Paxton.

While Paxton has minimized his criticism of Cornyn following their runoff, the private remarks demonstrate how their long-running tensions continue to roil the race, coming as national Republicans mount an all-out effort to help Paxton defeat Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. With polls showing a tight race, Republicans have poured well over $100 million into the general election in Texas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994 but is now critical to Republican hopes of holding a Senate majority.

‘He wants me to lose’: Paxton complains about lack of support from Cornyn in leaked audio

Source: CNN

Paxton made the comments at a September 24 gathering in Washington after receiving a question about Rep. Jasmine Crockett, the Democratic congresswoman whom Talarico defeated in his primary, according to two sources familiar with the discussion. The recording obtained by CNN begins with Paxton apparently referencing Crockett, who has not campaigned for Talarico, saying he does not “know how much she really affects votes.”

“I mean maybe a little bit around the margins, just like Cornyn, basically how much he affects me,” Paxton said.

After saying Cornyn wants him to lose, Paxton pointed to a recent encounter that he said a friend had with the senator at a Dallas restaurant. Paxton said the friend bought Cornyn’s table dessert and sought to thank him for “supporting the ticket” — and for “supporting Ken Paxton” — and Cornyn reacted angrily.

“Cornyn’s face went red. He backed off,” Paxton said. “He said, ‘Paxton’s gonna lose. We need to teach those Republicans a lesson. It’s going to be hard to learn, but they need to know that their decisions have consequences.’”

“That’s what he’s trying to do,” Paxton said. “That’s John Cornyn.”

CNN has not independently confirmed Paxton’s account, and a Cornyn representative, Rob Jesmer, told CNN that the conversation at the restaurant did not happen.

“If Sen. Cornyn wanted Ken to lose, I can assure you he’d be more active in the campaign,” Jesmer, a longtime political strategist for Cornyn, said. “He has said he supports the Republican ticket. Given all Ken has said and done, I think that’s a pretty good place for Sen. Cornyn to be.”

Asked for comment on the audio, Paxton’s campaign dismissed it as “a story that doesn’t exist” but noted that Paxton “has called, texted, and offered to have a conversation with Senator Cornyn.”

“Like all Texans, General Paxton appreciates his decades of service to the Lone Star State,” Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement. “We hope he will join us in our fight to preserve the institution that is the United States Senate and help save our majority.”

The two lobbyists who hosted the fundraising event, Chris Brinson and Susan Hirschmann, did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Talarico’s campaign.

A spokesperson for Crockett said she has taken a different approach than Cornyn since losing her own primary.

“Cornyn is the sitting senator and continues to attack his party’s nominee,” the spokesperson, Karrol Rimal, said in a statement. “Crockett endorsed Talarico on March 4th and has not stopped working to support Democrats across the nation since.”

Continued problems for Paxton’s campaign

Paxton’s problems with his own base, including former Cornyn supporters, have loomed over the final weeks of the race.

A Paxton campaign memo dated Tuesday, reported by Punchbowl News, told supporters that the “biggest challenge we face is shoring up Republicans following a bruising primary.”

A Fox News poll done late last month found that nearly a third of Republican likely voters had an unfavorable opinion of Paxton. While he was winning 90% of GOP voters, about a fifth of “non-MAGA” Republicans were breaking for Talarico.

The clip obtained by CNN is at least the fifth recording that has leaked from the fundraising event last month and put Paxton’s campaign on the defensive in the final weeks of the race. Previous clips have featured Paxton saying the GOP’s midterm convention damaged him politically and that he feels like he has lost “control” over his campaign as outside groups have handled most of the spending.

The road to the 2026 midterms starts now

  • Each week, Aaron Blake cuts through the political noise with sharp analysis of the races, candidates and trends that could decide control of Congress. Sign up for 20/26 Vision, a weekly newsletter focusing on this year’s midterms.

President Donald Trump, who backed Paxton in the primary, has said he is “worried” about the Texas race but largely declined to address the recordings when asked about them. He said Wednesday he was not second-guessing his endorsement.

“I would have no regrets at all,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

The president visited San Antonio on Wednesday night for a rally with Paxton where he praised him as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”

Years of bad blood

The bad blood between Cornyn and Paxton goes back years.

Cornyn, who served as Texas attorney general from 1999 to 2002, has long made clear that he believes Paxton has disgraced the office and served as an example of what happens when Republicans do not police their own. Paxton has dished it back, painting Cornyn as a relic of a bygone era of Republican politics in Texas, especially after Cornyn ushered through a bipartisan gun safety law in 2022.

Sen. John Cornyn, on Capitol Hill on August 4.

When Paxton faced a competitive primary for reelection in 2022, Cornyn did not make an endorsement but said Paxton’s long-running indictment on state securities fraud charges was an “embarrassment.” The case finally ended two years later with a deal where Paxton agreed to do community service and pay restitution.

After Paxton was acquitted in a state Senate impeachment trial in 2023, which centered on allegations he abused his office to help a donor, he wasted little time teasing a potential run against Cornyn in 2026. “Everything’s on the table,” he told former Fox News host Tucker Carlson in a triumphant interview days after the trial.

“Hard to run from prison, Ken,” Cornyn said in a February 2024 social media post after Paxton called for Texans to elect a new senator in 2026.

Paxton, who denies all wrongdoing, launched his campaign in April 2025 with a promise to “send John Cornyn packing.” Cornyn and allied groups unleashed tens of millions of dollars of bitter, negative ads against Paxton, some of them highlighting allegations of infidelity. Cornyn finished narrowly ahead of Paxton in the primary but did not earn enough support to avoid a runoff against Paxton.

“I refuse to allow a flawed, self-centered and shameless candidate like Ken Paxton to risk everything we’ve worked so hard to build over these many years,” Cornyn said on primary night, adding, “Judgment Day is coming for Ken Paxton.”

But Trump ultimately had other plans. He endorsed Paxton a week before the runoff, dealing a crushing blow to Cornyn and his hopes of stopping a fellow Republican who, to him, embodied much of what is wrong with the modern GOP.

‘He was not my first choice’

Cornyn had long promised to support the “Republican ticket” regardless of the outcome of the primary. But since losing, he has avoided helping Paxton and even leaned into his frustrations with the nominee and his wing of the party at times.

The senator criticized Paxton as a “poor campaigner” and “lazy” candidate in an August interview with the Texas Tribune. Cornyn and former President George W. Bush headlined a fundraiser in Dallas last month for six Senate GOP candidates in battleground races – but not Paxton.

Cornyn’s refusal to endorse Paxton has annoyed some Texas GOP leaders, including Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a top Trump ally in the state. Patrick suggested in June, following the primary runoff, that Cornyn was part of “sore losers undermining our party.”

Talarico, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to people who supported Cornyn in the GOP primary. He told CNN last month that he hopes to “live up to” Cornyn’s legacy and that he welcomes the incumbent’s supporters to “join this movement we’re building.”

The Democrat’s campaign even hired a former staffer in Cornyn’s office over the summer. Cornyn defended the staffer’s move amid some intraparty backlash, saying on X that “those concerned might want to channel their energy into broadening R[epublican] outreach.”

Some prominent supporters of Cornyn from the primary continue to show reluctance about voting for Paxton.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Ken Paxton during a campaign rally in San Antonio on October 7.

“I’m supporting the party, but he was not my first choice, and I do think it’s going to have an impact down-ballot,” Rep. Michael McCaul of Texas told CNN last month. “And I do think there are Republicans … that may just not vote, and that’s the danger.”

Paxton has made some headway with his intra-party opponents. In the weeks after the primary runoff, he was joined on the campaign trail by state Rep. Jeff Leach, who endorsed Cornyn in the primary and served as a leader in the 2023 impeachment case against Paxton.

Yet some Texas Republicans continue to worry that GOP voters could simply skip the race. Ken Paxton’s estranged wife, Angela Paxton, addressed that possibility during a recent speech to a group of GOP women, urging them to set aside their reservations with any particular candidate for the good of the party.

“When you can’t vote for, then vote against,” she said, “but vote.”

data.title: Some of RFK Jr.'s supporters are turning against him and Trump over 'broken promises'
data.description:
EXCLUSIVE
Health news
Health news

MAHA loyalists accuse Trump administration of ‘broken promises’

A scorecard from MAHA activists suggests the Trump administration has broken most of its promises to the movement. The “burn feels especially raw,” one prominent activist said.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Oct. 8, 2026, 12:43 PM EDT
By Julie Tsirkin and Aria Bendix

Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

“We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

“What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.”

“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

“To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.”

“I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.”

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

“What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said.

Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Phasing out food dyes

Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?”

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

“If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

“The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”

data.title: DOJ trying to indict former White House aide who testified about Jan. 6
data.description:
Politics

DOJ trying to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, who testified about Jan. 6

By
Sarah N. Lynch
Senior Justice Department Reporter
Sarah N. Lynch is the senior Justice Department reporter for CBS News, based in Washington, D.C.
Read Full Bio
Sarah N. Lynch,
Jacob Rosen
Justice Department Reporter
Jake Rosen is a reporter covering the Department of Justice. He was previously a campaign digital reporter covering President Trump's 2024 campaign and also served as an associate producer for "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Read Full Bio
Jacob Rosen

Updated on: October 8, 2026 / 6:24 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Federal prosecutors have been presenting evidence to a grand jury in Washington, D.C., on whether former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson may have lied to Congress in her testimony related to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Hutchinson, a former aide to White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, drew the ire of President Trump's base when she testified in 2022 before the House committee tasked with investigating the 2021 Capitol attack.

In a series of depositions and public committee testimony, she said that Mr. Trump and Meadows had been warned on Jan. 6 that some of his supporters were carrying weapons to the Capitol, but that Mr. Trump said he didn't care and tried to order officials to remove the magnetometers.

She also relayed a story she said was told to her by then-White House deputy chief of staff Tony Ornato, in which Mr. Trump grew incensed after his lead Secret Service agent declined to drive him to the Capitol after the president had delivered a speech to supporters. During that address on the White House Ellipse, he had encouraged them to go to the Capitol, where Congress was confirming the Electoral College results from the 2020 election. He told his supporters that "after this, we're going to walk down, and I'll be there with you."

Hutchinson testified that Ornato had told her that Mr. Trump lunged at the steering wheel.

Her account was later contradicted by Mr. Trump's driver, who in sworn testimony claimed that the president never tried to grab the steering wheel.

CBS News could not determine precisely which parts of Hutchinson's testimony are being scrutinized by prosecutors. According to media reports, Republican allies in the House of Representatives made the referral to the Justice Department.

CBS News has reached out to Hutchinson's counsel for comment.

In an unusual move, the Civil Rights Division — and not the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C. — is handling the Hutchinson investigation, sources said. It was not immediately clear why that office was assigned the case.

The recent flurry of grand jury activity in the investigation was first reported by Punchbowl News.

data.title: The midterms could make or break these politicians' 2028 presidential ambitions
data.description:
The midterms stakes are high for these 2028 presidential prospects

STEVE PEOPLES, JILL COLVIN and JOEY CAPPELLETTI
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 11:07 AM UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

NEW YORK (AP) — As most of the political world focuses on next month's midterm elections, the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view.

Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties' candidates — and their own White House ambitions.

Here's a closer look at some of the leading prospects and how their political futures may be influenced by what happens Nov. 3.

Newsom has a Southern strategy

Gavin Newsom leaves the California governor's office at the end of the year, and he's been among the most active Democrats throughout the midterms.

Advertisement

He's paid particular attention to the South, where he's campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which hosts the party's first presidential primary contest in 2028.

The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom's Campaign for Democracy political action committee, which was established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to African American voters, who make up the heart of the Democratic base.

Newsom's star power — and his extensive email list — has strengthened his relationships with key Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where he's sent out fundraising emails that have generated a surge of donations in recent months.

Perhaps Newsom's biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander. The proposition, approved by California voters last year, created a new congressional map that may allow Democrats to pick up as many as five additional U.S. House seats in California this fall.

As a presidential candidate, the California governor could argue that he was on the front lines of the redistricting battle. But if Democrats do not win all five seats in his state, Newsom's message could be muffled.

Vance's fate is tied to Trump

No potential candidate's fate is as closely tied to President Donald Trump and Republicans' performance as Vice President JD Vance.

The 42-year-old has embarked on an aggressive midterm campaign schedule — from the Midwest, to the South, to Alaska — and focused on the administration's efforts to root out fraud.

A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance's seat in 2025, is facing an aggressive challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in the governor's race, Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be scrutinized. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organization's new leader, has already endorsed Vance's potential presidential bid and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign.

Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but "trying to help elect Republicans."

Shapiro is all about Pennsylvania

Among the Democrats leading the 2028 conversation, none have done less beyond their home state than Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. He hasn't visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state.

That's by design for a 53-year-old Democrat whose selling point as a presidential candidate might be his clout in Pennsylvania, which has emerged as perhaps the most important swing state in the nation.

Shapiro is expected to cruise to reelection over his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, which has allowed him to spend his political capital elsewhere.

Shapiro has gone all in to ensure Democrats win both chambers of the state legislature in November, and he's devoted significant time and resources to flipping four congressional seats.

If Shapiro can demonstrate strength in swing counties like Beaver, Luzerne or Erie, it could help him make a credible claim to winning back some of the working-class voters that Democrats have lost in the Trump era.

Beshear faces risk and reward

As chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear may have done more than any other potential candidate to boost his national profile during the midterms. He'll headline a get-out-the-vote tour through key states, beginning with Nevada on Oct. 22.

He also spent some of the campaign on a national book tour, allowing him to cozy up to influential Democrats in early states.

Still, Beshear's spending decisions as chief of the governors association in 2026 may present the highest risk and reward for him heading into 2028.

He's been active in supporting Democratic candidates in traditional swing states like Wisconsin, Michigan and Arizona while pushing into Republican-leaning states like Ohio and Iowa, places he argues could be critical in the next White House campaign.

But Democrats in other states are clamoring for more resources and warning Beshear of blowback if he doesn't deliver. Under pressure, the governors association sent $1 million this week to help the candidate for Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa.

Cruz hits the road

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz has long been one of his party's most active campaigners and fundraisers, continuing those efforts this year as he openly weighs another presidential bid.

His Truth and Courage PAC has spent more than $2.4 million this year on ads supporting midterm candidates, according to AdImpact, mostly to help Senate candidate Ken Paxton in his home state.

Cruz has traveled three times to Iowa, the first state on Republicans' nominating calendar and where he won the caucuses during the 2016 primary. He'll be in Alaska next week, and is also planning trips to South Carolina, North Carolina and most likely Michigan.

Pritzker's money plays

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is seeking his third term in November, but the Democrat has focused more on helping midterm candidates in other states.

Pritzker's team says the billionaire Democrat has already donated $38 million to the party's midterm efforts, including personal donations and roughly $20 million through his Ready for the Fight PAC, which is focused on taking down MAGA candidates, even in long shot districts.

More than other 2028 prospects, Pritzker has been focused on the Texas governor's race, where he donated $1 million this week, on top of $200,000 he gave earlier. He's also been active on the speaker circuit, having participated in more than 75 events across the country, including in Nevada and New Hampshire. He's expected to visit South Carolina before Election Day as well.

AOC's progressive politics face a test

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has been increasingly open about a potential presidential run, where she would be a major player in the Democratic Party's progressive lane.

But first, she's trying to prove that her brand of politics can succeed in a presidential swing state like Michigan, where she has thrown her weight behind Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. They appeared together this week at a New York City fundraiser, and she cast his campaign as a broader test for the progressive movement.

"If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere," Ocasio-Cortez told the audience.

Ocasio-Cortez and other Democrats have acknowledged that she'll face questions about whether she can appeal to voters across the country. Ocasio-Cortez argues an El-Sayed victory in Michigan, which is one of the early states in the next Democratic presidential primary, could challenge some of those assumptions.

Buttigieg keeps a busy schedule

Since leaving his job as transportation secretary under President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg has had the luxury of free time. He has used it to aggressively travel across the country, raising money and campaigning for Democrats on the ballot this year.

Buttigieg has endorsed nearly 100 candidates this cycle, from state legislative contests to U.S. Senate races, and has appeared on the campaign trail with roughly half of them, according to his team. He has visited 37 states since leaving office.

The range of those appearances also offers a glimpse at Buttigieg's appeal within the party.

Democrats have welcomed him even in deeply Republican territory, including Nancy Lacore, a U.S. House candidate in South Carolina who campaigned with Buttigieg in August. He also helped bring Democratic candidates together for a Michigan unity event in August after hotly contested primaries.

data.title: Mamdani demands Trump end NYC ICE operations after agent shoots man with child in car
data.description:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants President Donald Trump to put an end to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s operations in the city after an agent-involved shooting injured one person on Thursday.

“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said in a statement Thursday evening. “I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities.”

Advertisement

New York police said that around 4 p.m., federal agents got involved in a shooting and injured a man in the city’s Marble Hill residential section. The police’s afternoon statement said the shooting victim was conscious and receiving medical attention in a nearby hospital.

But at a press conference Thursday evening before furious protesters, Mamdani said that after his two-hour conversation with Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he has failed to negotiate the release of the shooting victim.

The response to the shooting incident tests Mamdani’s charm offensive with the President, who appears unlikely to budge on his immigration agenda despite previous friendliness with the Democratic mayor. Despite wide ideological differences, Trump and Mamdani have had a cordial relationship.

Mamdani, however, remains just as firm on his own side of the issue. A steadfast critic of ICE operations, he has backed calls to abolish the agency. “I have said this directly—whether to the President or to the public—ICE undermines public safety,” he said.

Advertisement

The White House pointed TIME to the Department of Homeland Security’s statement, which attacked New York’s “sanctuary politicians” that limit cooperation with federal agents. “When dangerous illegal aliens are released back onto the streets by radical sanctuary politicians, our officers are forced to make arrests at large in the community in unpredictable and dangerous environments,” DHS posted on social media. 

Besides Mamdani, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, released a swift rebuke of the shooting and said she too spoke with Trump and Mullin. “New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity,” the governor said. “Federal authorities need to provide answers, and they must do so immediately.”

What happened?

City police commissioner Jessica Tisch said that based on initial information, police received multiple 911 calls around 4 p.m. reporting shots fired and a person shot near 2 Marble Hill Avenue.

Their preliminary investigation showed that federal immigration agents were “conducting a targeted enforcement operation” to take a person in a gray vehicle into custody. Their target, whom Tisch identified as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, was with a 5-year-old boy, whom police believed to be his son. 

Tisch said that one plainclothes federal agent approached the driver’s side window, with his gun drawn, with another plainclothes agent near the headlight, before the vehicle moved forward. According to evidence collected on the scene, Tisch said that at least one ICE agent fired seven rounds, “striking the driver in the neck below his left ear.”

Advertisement

DHS said in its statement that an ICE officer “discharged his weapon” and injured its target, whom ICE agents immediately rendered aid to. “The incident remains under investigation,” the department added.

Tisch added that when New York police arrived on scene, they saw men in various clothes, including “at least one carrying a long gun.” Police also saw the injured Belgal “handcuffed and seated on the ground,” and they “immediately” placed him into a police vehicle and gave aid, before transporting him to New York-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in stable condition. The child, meanwhile, is safe and in the care of a family member, Tisch added. 

What do we know about the victim?

Tisch said that Belgal had two prior arrests in New York City: “one for robbery in 2023 in which he pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years probation; and one for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025, which is still pending.” 

Advertisement

DHS did not name Belgal, but it described the target of the ICE operation as a “criminal illegal” immigrant from the Dominican Republic “with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”

The department alleged the shooting victim had ties to the Trinitarios gang, which was involved in the shooting of an off-duty Customs and Border Protection officer last year. It added that police arrested the target on Dec. 7, 2023, “but was released into the community a few days later by reckless Democrat sanctuary policies that put American lives at risk.”

What have been the reactions?

The New York City shooting is just the latest in a spate of violent incidents involving federal immigration agents. Tallies from the New York Times and ABC News show more than 20 people shot, with at least six killed, including three U.S. citizens: Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Ruben Ray Martinez. 

Advertisement

Read More: These Two Brothers Are Fighting to Protect Immigrant Families After a Tragedy

The city has also become a hotspot for ICE-related activity. As Gothamist reported on Oct. 7, more than 8,800—or nearly half—of all ICE arrests in New York state during the second-term Trump Administration have happened in New York City’s five boroughs.

Lawmakers have since debated the nationwide enforcement of Trump’s immigration agenda, leading to funding battles and partial shutdowns of DHS.

Mamdani and other New York politicians took issue with how the ICE operation could have endangered a child. “There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old,” the New York mayor said in the press conference.

Rep. Ritchie Torres, who represents the Bronx, posted that “firing multiple rounds into a car with a child inside, on a busy residential street in the Bronx, is abhorrent and indefensible.”

Advertisement

Rep. Adriano Espaillat, the Democrat representing the district covering Upper Manhattan and parts of West Bronx, posted on social media that ICE has denied him as well as the victim’s family from visiting and checking on the victim. Espaillat said he met the victim’s 5-year-old son, “distraught and traumatized after witnessing this horrific event.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who represents New York and led the legislative standoff that temporarily blocked funding for DHS, called the shooting “deeply disturbing, especially amid reports that a child was in the car when shots were fired.” The senator called on DHS to release body camera footage and ensure independent investigations.

data.title: Former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
data.description:
Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in international justice

KOSTYA MANENKOV, MARK LEWIS and STEFANIE DAZIO
Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 4:03 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Nobel Peace

1 of 6
FILE - U.N. human rights chief Navanethem Pillay prior to the opening of a session of the Human Rights Council at the European headquarters of the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, June 18, 2012. (Salvatore Di Nolfi/Keystone via AP, File) (Salvatore Di Nolfi/Keystone via AP)

OSLO, Norway (AP) — The South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief Navi Pillay, who is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Pillay's work "is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world," said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, Chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, in announcing her win in Oslo, Norway.

Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S. President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of a U.N. commission she led that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Both leaders also have been highly critical of the institutions where Pillay has worked.

Advertisement

While her work has been global in scope, criticism often has been fiercely local, notably in places like Israel and in apartheid-era South Africa as she and peers took on some of the world's most painful and sensitive legal issues and most vulnerable populations.

Pillay, 85, received the news while attending the Nuremberg Forum, a gathering to discuss international law in Nuremberg, Germany, the location of the trials of Nazi war criminals that helped lay the foundations of international law.

"Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me," she said to a standing ovation. "You know, you don't want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this."

And joking, she added: "But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information."

She chaired an investigation that determined Israel committed genocide in Gaza

Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the U.N.-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

The commission also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defense minister "have incited the commission of genocide." Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the charges.

Pillay has repeatedly rejected accusations from critics who accused her of antisemitism or allegedly turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel.

In an interview with the AP last year, she recalled how she worked closely with some Jewish lawyers in the fight against apartheid in her native South Africa and was invited to Israel as the U.N. rights chief from 2008 to 2014.

Her win puts the focus on a court under pressure from Trump

Pillay's win brings renewed attention to U.S. President Donald Trump's ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court. The Trump administration already has sanctioned 13 of the ICC's staff members, among them key prosecutors and nine judges including the court's Japanese President Tomoko Akane.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has launched what he called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."

In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump called the court an "out of control institution" and an "anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction" over the U.S. as he urged member states to quit the "rogue institution immediately."

There are fears the court as a whole could be sanctioned, a move that could seriously hamper its ability to mete out justice.

The Norwegian committee said it sought to strengthen international law at a time of conflict.

Watne Frydnes said the award was a message to those seeking to undermine "the international rules based system and the institutions."

"At a time when the number of wars and conflicts is rising, and when judges and institutions of international law are under political attack, the Nobel Committee wishes to issue a reminder that the ability to resolve conflicts without force or violence is dependent on the international rule of law," the committee wrote in a news release.

"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world."

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, the highest court of the United Nations, in the ongoing genocide case against Myanmar.

When countries do not have a national on the court's permanent, 15-judge panel, they can appoint an expert of their choice. Gambia, which launched the proceedings in 2019, selected Pillay when the country accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority group.

There were nearly 300 nominations for this year's prize

The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year's prize, with just over a quarter of them organizations. Experts say the committee typically focuses on the durability of peace, the promotion of international fraternity and the quiet work of institutions that strengthen those goals.

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness."

Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

The Peace prize follows a week of Nobel announcements

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

___

Dazio reported from Berlin and Lewis reported from Stavanger, Norway.

___

data.title: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
data.description:
2026 Election

Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate

Facing questions about gas prices, the war in Iran and tariffs, the candidates frequently exchanged insults amid a high-stakes campaign.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Oct. 8, 2026, 8:42 PM EDT
By Henry J. Gomez

GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.

Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs.

Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks.

“I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point.

Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election.

Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist.

The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly.

“I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.”

Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise.

“It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.”

At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.”

Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump.

New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war.

“I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.”

El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households.

“Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.”

El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”

The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.”

“I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.”

El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer.

“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied.

“We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”

The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts, with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game.

Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith.

Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed. And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”

Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name.

“Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.”

He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.”

data.title: Man hospitalized in New York shooting involving federal agents, NYPD says
data.description:
New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says

By Julia Harte and Kristina Cooke
Thu, October 8, 2026 at 11:56 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Shooting involving US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Bronx borough, in New York City

1 of 3
Members of law enforcement gather near a vehicle at the scene of a shooting reportedly involving US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in the Bronx borough of New York City, US, October 8, 2026. REUTERS/David Dee Delgado

By Julia Harte and Kristina Cooke

NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child ‌present in the vehicle in the Bronx borough of New York City, according to ‌the mayor, city police and eyewitness accounts.

"Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old-child in his car before firing multiple ​rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.

Advertisement

The mayor said the child was believed to have been physically unharmed. He referred to the man shot as a "New Yorker."

"This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mamdani said, adding he had called President Donald Trump to talk about the incident. "When we speak ‌I will demand that he ends ⁠all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities."

ICE did not immediately respond to a request from ⁠Reuters for comment on the incident.

The incident was first reported on X by the New York Police Department, which gave few details other than to say: "there was a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents," and that ​the person ​shot was "currently conscious and receiving medical attention."

The shooting ​occurred at around 4 p.m. ET (2000 GMT) ‌in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, the NYPD said.

An NYPD spokesperson said the agents involved in the shooting were part of DHS, the parent agency for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Customs and Border Protection and Border Patrol agencies, among others, and that federal authorities were investigating.

Pedro Almarez, owner of a nearby eatery, said he was working at the restaurant when he heard shots fired and ‌went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at ​the scene.

"There were a lot of ICE officers, three or ​four cars," Almarez told Reuters by phone, ​adding the man who was shot appeared to be between 20 and 30 ‌years of age. He said NYPD officers ​arrived about 10 minutes later.

The ​city police department said its officers were not involved in the shooting.

At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing ​on a balcony overlooking the area ‌was heckling officers below about "taking our children."

(Reporting by Julia Harte in New York; Additional ​reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; Writing and additional reporting by Steve Gorman in ​Los Angeles; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and Chris Reese)

data.title: Long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
data.description:
U.S. & World

Historic homecoming: Sea-weary, battle-tested USS Lincoln arrives in San Diego

Aircraft carrier is back at its California homeport after 10-plus months at sea while enduring combat and other difficulties

Published: Oct 8, 2026, 2:56 p.m. MDT
See More Deseret News Stories In Search
View 2 Comments
Share
By Jason Swensen
Jason writes for the Deseret News’ politics and the West team covering education, the military and faith-based sports stories.
NEW: Try Article Audio
NEW: Try Article Audio
Audio quality:|
00:00
00:00
1.0x
00:00/00:00
-
+
KEY POINTS
  • The USS Lincoln arrived at its San Diego homeport Thursday after an almost 11-month deployment that included combat in the Middle East.
  • Massive crowds welcomed home the thousands of sailors and Marines serving on the aircraft carrier.
  • The Lincoln's long deployment — and the accounts of several challenges aboard the ship — has prompted calls for congressional hearings.

“Home is the sailor, home from sea.”

Robert Louis Stevenson penned that line almost 150 years ago — but on Thursday, those words read sweet and new to thousands of sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

After an almost 11-month deployment to the Middle East, the sea-weary aircraft carrier arrived at its homeport at San Diego’s Naval Air Station North to massive crowds of cheering, misty-eyed and flag-waving spouses, children, parents, friends and fellow troops.

The massive ship played a pivotal combat role during the ongoing Iran war — setting a record-long deployment of more than 260 uninterrupted days at sea that included two extensions.

The USS Lincoln arrived in San Diego Bay late Thursday morning under unseasonably warm skies. Scores of sailors and Marines, dressed in service dress uniforms, lined the carrier’s flight deck to the delight of awaiting loved ones.

The deployment’s historic length — coupled with reports of stark conditions during combat — brought wide attention to the USS Lincoln and its crew.

And while the carrier is now far from the Middle East, the scrutiny of its 2025-2026 deployment will continue. Accounts of suicide attempts, food rationing, broken plumbing and mental health emergencies prompted Democratic lawmakers to call for a congressional hearing.

President Donald Trump labeled reports of dire conditions about the USS Lincoln as “a CNN fake report” — and refuted that relatives of the Lincoln sailors had raised concerns about the carrier’s length at sea, saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough,” The Associated Press reported.

And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in August that conditions aboard the Lincoln were “completely misrepresented.”

But Navy leaders later acknowledged issues aboard a “city at sea” that thousands called home while underway. Meanwhile, experts told The Associated Press that the reported suicide attempts are a low number in a strike group of 6,000 sailors at sea for over 10 months.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., requested the congressional hearing following a Sept. 22 letter from Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirming that eight suicide attempts were made during the Lincoln group’s combat-heavy deployment.

“Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect,” wrote Gillibrand, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

“That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”

Americans, she added, need hearings, accountability, and “a clear plan to protect our service members and prioritize American families.”

Hegseth: A ‘generational mission’ for the USS Lincoln

While the Lincoln sailors had to wait until Thursday to finally step on terra firma, Hegseth flew on a helicopter to the carrier Wednesday to get an early jump on the “welcome homes.”

“I’m here today on behalf of the President of the United States to make sure you understand how deeply grateful we are — and how much we want to showcase and recognize the historic undertaking of this strike group,” said Hegseth.

Related
"State of the Force': Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivers combative address — renewing calls for the 'warrior ethos'

The secretary announced that Trump was presenting the USS Abraham Carrier Strike Group with the Presidential Unit Citation — the highest collective unit award in the American military.

Hegseth also saluted the Lincoln carrier group’s “back of the baseball card” statistics that included almost 11 months at sea, two extensions in the middle of a combat zone, over 10,000 flights and 23,000 flight hours, 1.5 million pounds of ordnance dropped and 64 Iranian Navy ships sunk.

“You were called upon by your nation for an important and significant and generational mission to ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” added Hegseth. “Theocratic regimes should never have access to nuclear weapons. President Trump recognizes that — and he called upon the Lincoln from day one to execute on that.”

The Iranians and the United States made a deal to share the ocean, he joked. “The Iranian Navy gets the bottom of the ocean — and the Lincoln gets the top.”

Since the beginning of the Iran war, Hegseth has been frequently critical of the media’s coverage of the conflict. He once again scolded the press during his Wednesday visit to the Lincoln.

“There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol — a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission,” he said.

“And when I look at (the crew), and when I talk to your leadership. … I know it’s the exact opposite, which is actually what the media does so often.”

The families and loved ones of the Lincoln sailors, added Hegseth, have also performed honorably during the long deployment.

“When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass along my gratitude from the president and myself,” he told the troops. “Let them know that their long wait was in service of a righteous and historic mission. Thank them for their patience, for their patriotism, for their love, for their support and for pitching in on the homeland, which is never easy.”

Lincoln’s sailors reflect on nearly a year at sea

As the 1,092-foot-long vessel was navigating towards the U.S. mainland on Wednesday, many Lincoln sailors told the San Diego Union-Tribune that they were not always aware of the broad news coverage at home because Wi-Fi communication on the ship was sometimes limited.

Roman Elliott, a 20-year-old mechanic’s mate, said, with a smile, “I learned to deal with it by playing cards. Lots of cards.

“I am a little nervous about the (homecoming). It’s kind of like things were at the end of boot camp, when you’re finally free,” he added. “I’m looking forward to that.”

Christian Webster, a 22-year-old aviation repair worker, had a different take, telling the San Diego Union-Tribune that he never thought he would see combat when he joined the military.

“This is going to stay with me, knowing that I went through and accomplished what I want to do, and that I have gone far.”

Meanwhile, sailor Steven Rivas learned firsthand the sacrifices that are often asked of American service personnel during times of war. His wife, Brenda, gave birth to their daughter during the historic Lincoln deployment.

But Rivas didn’t find out he was a new dad for more than a week after Baby Evie’s birth because the Lincoln crew was not allowed to use Wi-Fi at the time to send messages.

“I had no way to find out if there were any complications,” Rivas said Wednesday in a San Diego Union-Tribune interview. “It was just a waiting game for me to find out. When I finally did see pictures of (Evie) I, well, I cried. My wife said the birth was a real snap.”

Rivas and his wife are not alone. The babies of scores of Lincoln crew members were reportedly delivered during the carrier group’s deployment.
